details:
**The Four Seasons (Antonio Vivaldi)**
Vivaldi's set of four violin concertos, "Spring," "Summer," "Autumn," and "Winter," which make up the first four of the twelve concertos in his collection The Contest Between Harmony and Invention. They were published with sonnets, likely by Vivaldi himself, describing the natural scenes the music depicts; Vivaldi wrote hundreds of violin concertos in total.

**Barking dog (the "Spring" concerto)**
In the slow movement of "Spring," the violas play a repeated two-note figure marked always loud, representing a barking dog, while the solo violin depicts a sleeping goatherd. The concerto ends with a rustic dance imitating bagpipes, and philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau arranged "Spring" for solo flute.

**Thunderstorm and sleeping drunkards (Four Seasons scenes)**
The Presto finale of "Summer" uses rapid repeated notes to depict a violent thunderstorm. "Autumn" includes a languid harpsichord passage showing drunkards falling asleep after a harvest festival and a hunt in which a stag is killed, while "Winter" uses pizzicato strings to depict rain on a window.

**Modern versions of The Four Seasons**
Astor Piazzolla wrote a tango-based suite, The Four Seasons of Buenos Aires, inspired by Vivaldi's set. Max Richter's 2012 "Recomposed" version was premiered by violinist Daniel Hope, and Nigel Kennedy's 1989 recording became one of the best-selling classical albums ever.

**24 Caprices (Niccolò Paganini)**
A set of extremely difficult solo violin pieces by the Italian virtuoso Paganini, who was rumored to have sold his soul to the devil. No. 9, "The Hunt," imitates flutes and horns; No. 13 is "The Devil's Laughter"; No. 6 is "The Trill"; and the theme of No. 24 inspired Rachmaninoff's Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini, among many other variation sets.

**"Devil's Trill" Sonata (Giuseppe Tartini)**
A famously difficult Baroque violin sonata that Tartini claimed was inspired by a dream in which the devil played the violin for him. It is named for the demanding trills in its final movement.

**Beethoven's Violin Concerto in D major**
Beethoven's only violin concerto, which opens with soft repeated timpani strokes before the oboes and other woodwinds present the first theme. It was neglected until Joseph Joachim revived it, and it has been recorded by violinists such as Jascha Heifetz and Itzhak Perlman.

**Brahms's Violin Concerto in D major**
A concerto written for and dedicated to Joseph Joachim, whose cadenza is usually played. Brahms replaced two planned middle movements with what he called a "feeble adagio" opening with a long oboe solo, and Pablo de Sarasate refused to play the piece because he did not want to stand on stage while the oboe played the only tune in the adagio.

**Mendelssohn's Violin Concerto in E minor**
A concerto whose soloist enters almost immediately with an opening melody that Mendelssohn said gave him "no peace." Joachim called it "the heart's jewel" among German violin concertos, and it was a signature piece of Yehudi Menuhin.

**"Kreutzer" and "Spring" sonatas (Beethoven)**
Beethoven's best-known violin sonatas. The A major "Kreutzer" Sonata was premiered by violinist George Bridgetower before Beethoven rededicated it to Rodolphe Kreutzer, and the F major Sonata No. 5 is nicknamed "Spring."

**Other violin sonatas: Franck, F-A-E, and Ysaÿe**
César Franck's A major Violin Sonata was premiered by Belgian virtuoso Eugène Ysaÿe, who himself wrote six sonatas for solo violin; his second opens by quoting the Preludio of Bach's E major Partita No. 3. The "F-A-E" Sonata was a joint work by Robert Schumann, Johannes Brahms, and Albert Dietrich for Joachim, based on his motto "Frei aber einsam."

**Stradivarius violins and famous violinists**
The violins made by Antonio Stradivari are the most prized in the world; Paganini played one, and "The Soil" Stradivarius was owned by Yehudi Menuhin and later Itzhak Perlman, the polio-stricken soloist on the Schindler's List soundtrack. Joshua Bell once busked incognito in a Washington, D.C. Metro station as a Washington Post experiment, and Shinichi Suzuki, founder of the Suzuki method, was a violinist.

**Highest-pitched string instrument and the concertmaster**
The violin is the smallest and highest-pitched member of the orchestral string family, with its highest string tuned to E, and it is the most numerous instrument in a standard orchestra. The orchestra's concertmaster is the principal first violinist.

**"Turkish" Concerto (Mozart's Violin Concerto No. 5 in A major)**
The last of Mozart's five violin concertos. Its first movement, marked "Allegro aperto," is briefly interrupted by a short Adagio passage for the soloist, and its finale contains a "Turkish"-style section imitating Janissary music.

**Sibelius's Violin Concerto in D minor**
Sibelius's only concerto, a staple of the violin repertoire. Critic Donald Tovey described its rhythmically heavy finale as a "polonaise for polar bears."
